intent: I'm choosing a numerical scheme to solve Parker's cosmic-ray transport equation in 3D. People keep telling me to use stochastic differential equations (SDEs) instead of finite-difference / ADI grid solvers, and to run the SDEs on a GPU or a large cluster. Walk me through the concrete tradeoffs: in what regime do SDEs win over finite differences, what are the actual measured speedups (GPU vs CPU, and HPC scaling), what does the time-backward pseudo-particle formulation buy you, and where do grid-based ADI methods still have an advantage? I want the engineering tradeoff, not a sales pitch for one method.
nuggets: SDE methods recast Parker's transport equation into an equivalent set of stochastic differential equations integrated over many independent pseudo-particle trajectories, are unconditionally stable, and avoid the spatial grid and matrix inversions that ADI finite-difference solvers require

The time-backward formulation releases pseudo-particles from the observation point to the boundary, which is far more efficient than time-forward when intensities are needed at only a few phase-space points (Dunzlaff2015)

Because pseudo-particle trajectories are independent, the problem is embarrassingly parallel; GPU implementations report ~12-60x speedup over multi-threaded CPU (Dunzlaff2015) and cluster implementations scale to thousands of cores (Moloto2019)

Kopp2012 provides a general modular SDE code for 4-6 dimensional Fokker-Planck problems in Cartesian/cylindrical/spherical coordinates and validates it against an established finite-difference code, showing agreement on a problem with sources and a linear loss term

Pei2010 demonstrates that integrating directly in spherical coordinates (avoiding coordinate transforms) makes the SDE code substantially more efficient and that Ito's theorem guarantees equivalence to Parker's equation

A residual advantage of grid/finite-difference solvers is that they yield the full phase-space distribution in one solve, whereas SDEs need re-running per output point unless a transition-probability / boundary-independent formulation is used (Effenberger2017 review)

intent: I keep reading opposite conclusions about whether the nearby pulsars Geminga and B0656+14 explain the AMS-02/PAMELA cosmic-ray positron excess. The same HAWC TeV gamma-ray halo measurement is used to argue BOTH that pulsars dominate the positron flux AND that they cannot. Reconcile the disagreement: what does the measured halo extension imply about the diffusion coefficient, which physical assumption flips the conclusion, and what do follow-up analyses (Fermi-LAT halo, inhomogeneous diffusion) say?
nuggets: HAWC measured ~2-degree extended TeV gamma-ray halos around Geminga and B0656+14, implying a diffusion coefficient near the sources ~10^2-10^3 times smaller than the typical ISM value (near-Bohm)

Abeysekara2017 concludes that, under homogeneous isotropic diffusion, this slow diffusion prevents the pulsars' positrons from reaching Earth in sufficient quantity, so they are UNLIKELY to be the dominant source of the excess

Hooper2017 uses the same HAWC/Milagro data with a different transport treatment and concludes the pulsars INVARIABLY produce a positron flux similar in spectrum and magnitude to the observed excess, favoring the pulsar interpretation

Profumo2018 shows the conclusion is driven by the homogeneous-diffusion assumption: a radially-dependent (spatially inhomogeneous) diffusion coefficient, slow only inside the nebula, lets the pulsars match the positron flux, dissolving the Abeysekara2017 exclusion

Mauro2019 detects a Fermi-LAT GeV gamma-ray halo around Geminga, infers a diffusion coefficient ~1.1e27 cm^2/s at 100 GeV and ~1% spin-down-to-pair conversion efficiency, and estimates Geminga contributes at most ~20% of the highest-energy AMS-02 positrons, consistent with cumulative Galactic pulsars explaining the excess

intent: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 both crossed the heliopause, but the cosmic-ray and heliosheath observations at the two crossings were notably different, and numerical modulation models make specific predictions for what should happen along each trajectory out to the heliopause. Compare the two crossings (timing, distance, boundary-layer structure, precursor phenomena, ACR persistence) and explain which of those differences are reproduced or predicted by heliosheath transport models versus which remain anomalies the models do not capture.
nuggets: Voyager 2 crossed the heliopause on 5 Nov 2018 at 119 au with a sharp simultaneous drop in heliospheric/ACR ions and rise in galactic cosmic rays (Stone2019); Voyager 1 crossed earlier in 2012 at ~122 au (Stone2013)

Unlike Voyager 1, which saw precursor interstellar flux tubes invading the heliosheath before crossing, Voyager 2 observed no such precursors, and the ACR mass/pitch-angle persistence seen at V1 was absent at V2, implying different field-gradient/diffusion conditions at the two crossings (Stone2019)

Just outside the heliopause Voyager 2 found a cosmic-ray boundary layer where GCR intensity was ~90% of the far value, i.e. GCRs remain modulated in a thin layer beyond the nominal heliopause (Stone2019)

Heliosheath transport models predict small GCR radial gradients in the heliosheath (e.g. ~1.5-1.8% per au at 180 MeV) and that the termination shock does not accelerate GCR ions efficiently, with the heliosheath acting as a significant modulation barrier for low-energy ions (Florinski2009)

Time-dependent modulation models compute GCR intensities along the actual Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 trajectories toward and beyond the heliopause, providing the model baseline against which the observed crossing differences are judged (Manuel2011)

intent: I want to understand the failure modes of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and how the proposed remedies relate to each other. Specifically: why do PINNs sometimes fail to train at all, what does the neural-tangent-kernel analysis say about which loss term dominates, how do adaptive loss-weighting / adaptive sampling / domain-decomposition remedies target different parts of the failure, and what does this imply for stiff or multi-scale PDEs like transport equations?
nuggets: Wang2021 derives the neural tangent kernel (NTK) of PINNs and shows a discrepancy in the convergence rates of the different loss components (PDE-residual vs boundary/data terms), which is a fundamental pathology causing some PINNs to fail to train, and proposes NTK-eigenvalue-based adaptive weighting to rebalance them

A distinct failure mode is spectral bias / inability to capture sharp or high-frequency features and stiff dynamics, which adaptive-sampling or residual-based point refinement targets by concentrating collocation points where the residual is large (Mao2023 high-speed-flow PINN)

Domain decomposition / extended-PINN approaches (XPINN/conservative PINN) target large or multi-scale domains by splitting them into subdomains with interface conditions, a different lever than loss-reweighting (Karniadakis2021 review framing)

Transfer learning / operator-learning remedies (Goswami2022) attack the cost and generalization failure by reusing trained representations across related problems rather than fixing the per-problem optimization landscape

For stiff / multi-scale PDEs the failure is dominated by the imbalance Wang2021 identifies plus spectral bias, so the effective remedy is a COMBINATION (adaptive weighting + adaptive sampling) rather than any single fix, and these levers are largely orthogonal

intent: I want to adjudicate the cosmic-ray spectral-hardening debate using ONLY the secondary-to-primary differential as the discriminating observable: lay out, quantitatively, why a break in the Galactic diffusion coefficient predicts that secondary nuclei (Li, Be, B) must harden exactly twice as much as primaries (He, C, O), what AMS-02 actually measured for that differential and at what rigidity, and why a pure source-injection break cannot produce a feature in secondary-to-primary ratios at all.
nuggets: Solving the transport equation, the primary disk spectrum scales as f_pri ~ E^-(Gamma_inj + delta) while the secondary spectrum (whose injection is the propagated primary spectrum) scales as f_sec ~ E^-(Gamma_inj + 2*delta), so any change in the diffusion-slope delta produces a spectral-index change in secondaries that is exactly TWICE that in primaries (Fornieri2021).

AMS-02 measured that above ~200 GV the secondary species (Li, Be, B) harden with a spectral-index change roughly twice as large as the primary species (He, C, O) - a >5 sigma effect (Aguilar2018a/Aguilar2020).
The Li/O secondary-to-primary ratio shows a break near ~192-200 GV where its log-slope changes from Delta ~= 0.45 to Delta ~= 0.25 (Tomassetti2023).

If the hardening originated from intrinsic properties of the CR accelerators (a source/injection break), NO feature should appear in the secondary-to-primary ratios; the observed break in those ratios is therefore a signature of a propagation/diffusion origin (Tomassetti2023; Schroer2021).

A Bayesian global fit to AMS-02 primary and secondary nuclei finds that BOTH a high-rigidity break in primary source injection AND a high-rigidity break in the diffusion coefficient can currently reproduce the spectra, and that more precise multi-TV secondary data are needed to distinguish them (Niu2019).

intent: When solving Parker's cosmic-ray transport equation numerically, finite-difference ADI schemes hit a hard dimensionality wall while stochastic-differential-equation (SDE) pseudo-particle solvers do not. Explain precisely what that wall is - up to how many dimensions ADI remains usable, why time-dependent 3D-spatial ADI specifically fails, and how the SDE approach sidesteps it - citing the concrete numerical-stability arguments.
nuggets: ADI (Alternating Direction Implicit) finite-difference methods become increasingly inaccurate or numerically unstable as the number of dimensions grows and cannot be applied beyond 4D (three spatial plus rigidity) without sacrificing time-dependence (Kopp2012).

ADI schemes treat the mixed second derivatives in the parabolic transport equation explicitly, which makes them unreliable for model-calculated 3D magnetic fields that produce strong anisotropy/non-uniformity in the transport coefficients (Florinski2013a).
SDE/pseudo-particle solvers are unconditionally (always) numerically stable, in contrast to finite-difference schemes that can go unstable for too-large time steps (Dunzlaff2015; Florinski2013a).

Because each pseudo-particle trajectory is independent, the SDE approach is embarrassingly parallel and uses very little memory (variables updated along trajectories rather than stored on a full grid) (Pei2010; Kopp2012).

SDE solvers compute the solution only at the phase-space point(s) of interest (e.g. a spectrum at Earth) whereas finite-difference solvers compute the distribution function over the whole grid; the time-backward SDE formulation is the efficient choice when intensities are needed at only a few points (Dunzlaff2015).

intent: In the AMS-02/PAMELA charge-sign solar-modulation literature, I want to reconcile how the SAME group's 3D Parker-equation drift model reproduces electrons+positrons (Aslam2020), antiprotons (Aslam2023), and the magnetic-reversal-period unfolding (Aslam2023a) using one consistent set of rigidity-dependent parallel/perpendicular mean free paths and a drift scale that drops to its minimum during polarity reversal. Specifically: how does the SAME drift-scale-minimal-at-reversal mechanism manifest differently for leptons vs antiprotons, and where does the model concede it cannot fix the polarity sign during 2012-2014?
nuggets: Aslam2020 reproduces PAMELA+AMS-02 e+/e- 2006-2015 and quantifies how much particle drift is needed in each solar-activity phase, finding no well-defined magnetic polarity (and thus an indeterminate drift pattern) during the Nov 2012-Mar 2014 reversal phase.

Aslam2023 simulates antiproton modulation over July 2006-Nov 2019 using proton-derived modulation parameters and finds the drift scale at its LOWEST and the mean free paths at their lowest during 2015 Mar-Apr (the post-reversal period), driving the p/antiproton ratio's charge-sign hysteresis loops.

Across Aslam2020 (leptons), Aslam2023 (antiprotons) and Aslam2023a (reversal unfolding), the common finding is that the drift coefficient must be scaled to a very small value during the HMF polarity-reversal interval to reproduce the data -- a single mechanism (suppressed drift at reversal) producing the lepton and antiproton charge-sign signatures.

Potgieter2021 independently reports the same suppression -- the drift coefficient must be reduced to a very small value during polarity reversal to reproduce AMS-02 -- corroborating the Aslam-group result with a separate full-drift model.

intent: I am writing a survey on data-driven equation discovery and want a single authoritative framing of how the field is CATEGORIZED -- the relationship between sparse-regression PDE discovery, PINN-based discovery, Bayesian/UQ discovery, and manifold/coordinate discovery -- under one unified mathematical framework, and what role statistics plays in making the identifiability problem rigorous. I want the review-level taxonomy, not individual method results.
nuggets: North2022 provides a categorization of data-driven discovery approaches and a UNIFIED mathematical framework showing the relationship between sparse-regression, neural-network, and Bayesian approaches, and argues for casting the discovery problem in a statistical framework to make identifiability tractable.

North2022 identifies identifiability -- whether the true response, true discrepancy, and noise can be uniquely determined -- as a key under-addressed challenge, exacerbated when different parameter/hyperparameter combinations explain the same data, requiring prior knowledge to resolve.

Hirsh2022 (UQ-SINDy) recasts SINDy coefficient estimation as sparse Bayesian inference, returning posterior distributions AND per-term inclusion probabilities (via spike-and-slab and regularized-horseshoe priors), discovering accurate models with orders-of-magnitude less data than point-estimate methods.

Nayek2021 uses spike-and-slab priors with a Gibbs sampler for Bayesian equation discovery of nonlinear structural-dynamic systems, achieving better model-selection consistency and fewer false discoveries than relevance-vector-machine sparsification.
